title: The 836-Day Hunt For Alvin Karpis, The Last Public Enemy
sources: FBI.gov History, Famous Cases & Criminals: Barker/Karpis Gang
FBI.gov New Orleans field office history; 'A Byte Out of History' (May 2012)
Wikipedia: Alvin Karpis; Barker-Karpis Gang; Ma Barker; Doc Barker; Ocklawaha, Florida
Hedged in script: Ma Barker's role (Karpis's claim), Old Joe (FBI history), Hoover's role in the arrest (disputed), necktie owner (disputed), Manson guitar (Karpis's account)

beats.text: New Orleans. A spring evening. A man walks out of an apartment on Canal Street and gets into a new Plymouth.
He has no idea that federal agents are hiding all around the block.
And one of them is the most famous lawman in America, a man who has never arrested anyone in his life.
This is Alvin Karpis. They call him Creepy, because of his cold, thin smile.
He is Public Enemy Number One. And tonight, his hunt ends in a way nobody expected.
To understand how it got here, we go back more than two years, to a cold morning in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
January 1934. A banker named Edward Bremer drops his daughter at school and stops at a corner.
A car blocks his path. Men with guns pull him out, hit him, and drive him away.
The ransom demand is two hundred thousand dollars. One of the biggest in American history at the time.
The men behind it are the Barker-Karpis gang, the same crew that kidnapped the brewer William Hamm the summer before.
That job paid a hundred thousand dollars. Hamm was released unharmed in Wisconsin, and the gang got away clean.
Why Saint Paul? For years the city ran an unwritten deal. Check in with the police, commit no crimes in town, and you could hide there in peace.
By 1934 that deal was breaking down. And the gang was now hitting the city's own rich families.
Karpis met Fred Barker in a Kansas prison. When they got out, they became partners.
He was born in Montreal to Lithuanian parents and grew up in Topeka, Kansas. He was stealing before he was a teenager.
Fred's mother, Kate, travelled with them. The press would call her Ma Barker.
For decades, newspapers painted her as the gang's evil brain. Karpis later insisted she never planned a single crime.
After three weeks, the family pays. Bremer is released alive near Rochester, Minnesota.
Now the case belongs to the Bureau of Investigation, and its young director, J. Edgar Hoover.

v.alt: United States Department of Justice building

beats.text: And in 1934, Congress finally gives its agents the power to carry guns and make arrests across the country. The hunt has real teeth now.
Agents go back over every step. They question Bremer about every sound and smell from his days blindfolded.
And they find fingerprints. Prints that point straight at Fred's brother, Arthur, known as Doc Barker.
The gang knows its faces and fingers are now its biggest weakness.
So Karpis and Fred Barker pay a crooked Chicago doctor named Joseph Moran to change them.
He cuts into their faces and tries to burn away their fingerprints.
It is agony. And it does not work. The prints grow back.
Not long after, Doctor Moran disappears. His body is never found. Many believe the gang silenced him.
The money is a problem too. Ransom bills have their serial numbers written down. Every one is a trail.
Across the country, people who swap the hot bills for clean money start getting arrested.
All through 1934, the net tightens. Dillinger is shot dead in Chicago. Baby Face Nelson is killed in November.
One by one, the big names fall. But Karpis is still out there.
January eighth, 1935. Agents surround Doc Barker outside an apartment in Chicago and arrest him without a shot.
With him they find a map of Florida. A lake is circled on it.
According to the FBI's own history, a letter mentioned a famous local alligator, called Old Joe.
Agents ask around. And they find a lakeside house at Ocklawaha, rented by a quiet mother and her son.
January sixteenth. At dawn, agents surround the house and call for the Barkers to come out.
The answer is gunfire. The shootout lasts for hours.
When it ends, Fred Barker and Ma Barker are both dead inside.
Karpis is not there. He is a thousand miles away, in Atlantic City.
Four days later, police knock on his hotel door there. Karpis shoots his way out into the night.
He leaves behind his girlfriend, Dolores Delaney, who is pregnant. She is arrested.
With the Barkers gone, Karpis is now the top name on the list. Public Enemy Number One.
And he does not hide quietly. In November 1935, his crew stops a mail train at Garrettsville, Ohio.
They walk off with tens of thousands of dollars. Then he vanishes again, to Hot Springs, Arkansas.
Meanwhile in Washington, the hunt turns personal.
April 1936. At a Senate hearing on his budget, Senator Kenneth McKellar asks Hoover a simple question.
Have you ever personally arrested anyone?

v.text: Did you ever make an arrest?

beats.text: Hoover has to admit it. No. He has run the Bureau for more than ten years, but never made an arrest himself.
The story goes that he leaves the hearing with one promise. When Karpis is found, he will be there.
Agents work the girlfriends, the bars, the doctors, the money. In Hot Springs, Karpis slips away again.
Then a tip comes in. He is in New Orleans, in an apartment on Canal Street.
Agents stake out the building. Hoover flies south to join them.
May first, 1936. Karpis and his partner Fred Hunter walk out and get into their car.
Agents rush in from both sides. Before Karpis can reach the rifle on the back seat, a hand is on him.
Hoover's version: the director himself grabs the most wanted man in America.
Karpis tells it very differently. He later said Hoover hid behind a building until agents had him, and only then stepped out.
And then the strangest detail. The story goes that nobody had brought handcuffs.
So they tie his hands with a necktie. Even today, at least four different men have been named as the owner of that tie.
Whoever owned it, the headlines the next day are all about one man. Hoover.
It is a turning point. The Bureau's agents become the G-Men, heroes of radio and film.
The Bureau already had a new name by then: the Federal Bureau of Investigation. After New Orleans, the whole country knew it.
Karpis is flown to Saint Paul. He pleads guilty to the Hamm kidnapping and gets life in prison.
That summer he is sent to a new federal prison on an island in San Francisco Bay. Alcatraz.
He stays there longer than any other prisoner in its history. About twenty-six years.
Doc Barker is there too. In 1939 he is shot dead trying to escape.
When Alcatraz begins to close, Karpis is moved to McNeil Island in Washington State.
By his own account, there he taught a young inmate to play the steel guitar. The inmate's name was Charles Manson.
In 1969 he is paroled and deported to Canada, where he was born.
He writes books about his life, and he never stops telling his version of the night in New Orleans.
In his memoir, he calls the arrest a show, staged so the director could finally say he caught someone.
He dies in Spain in 1979.
So who really caught Alvin Karpis?
Not one man. A fingerprint, a circled lake, an alligator named Old Joe, and marked bills changing hands across the country.
Piece by piece, eight hundred and thirty-six days of work.
And at the very end, a necktie, and a question in a Senate hearing room that Hoover never forgot.
